claims.claim: Bishop of Lycopolis who split from Peter of Alexandria over the lapsed, beginning the Melitian schism
claims.witness: Letter of the four bishops and of Peter (anf06); Epiphanius, Panarion 68; Athanasius, Defence against the Arians; Bell

claims.claim: Ordained clergy in other bishops' dioceses and in prison, against church order
claims.witness: The four bishops' letter and Peter's letter (anf06, contemporary)

claims.claim: The schism was over discipline, not doctrine
claims.witness: Bell; Robertson

claims.claim: Deposed by Peter for crimes including sacrificing to idols
claims.witness: Athanasius, Defence against the Arians 59 (a hostile witness); Bell doubts it

claims.claim: The Council of Nicaea (325) let him keep the title of bishop but forbade him to ordain
claims.witness: The council's letter in Socrates I.9

claims.claim: Near his death he named John as his successor, against the Nicene terms
claims.witness: Sozomen II; Bell

claims.claim: His followers called themselves the Church of the Martyrs and lasted into the eighth century
claims.witness: Epiphanius, Panarion 68; Bell (the later papyri and references)

contested_claims.claim: Melitius sacrificed to idols during the persecution
contested_claims.sides: Athanasius, Defence against the Arians 59, for (a hostile witness); H. Idris Bell against (the charge came readily to churchmen after a persecution)

absent_details.detail: His birth and the exact year of his death
absent_details.note: No held source gives either. He died after the Council of 325, since he named a successor against its terms.

claims.claim: A presbyter of Alexandria, in charge of the church of Baucalis, who also taught Scripture
claims.witness: Archibald Robertson, prolegomena to Athanasius (npnf204)

claims.claim: His answer to Bishop Alexander, that there was a time when the Son was not
claims.witness: Socrates I.5, writing more than a century later

claims.claim: Taught that the Son was made from nothing, yet subsisted before time as perfect God
claims.witness: Arius's own letter to Eusebius of Nicomedia (Theodoret I.4); the Thalia quoted by Athanasius

claims.claim: Wrote songs for sailors, millers and travellers, and the Thalia
claims.witness: Philostorgius II.2, through Photius's epitome (songs); Athanasius, Orations (ballads and the Thalia, which he quotes)

claims.claim: Condemned at Nicaea in 325; exiled, and his books ordered burned
claims.witness: Socrates I.8-9 (the synod's decision and Constantine's letter)

claims.claim: Alexander of Constantinople prayed against his reception, and Arius died suddenly the day before it
claims.witness: Athanasius, letter to Serapion, from the presbyter Macarius (Athanasius was not present); Robertson; Sozomen II.29-30

claims.claim: Died in 336
claims.witness: Robertson's chronology

contested_claims.sides: Socrates I.5: Arius's answer to Alexander's teaching on the Trinity; Constantine's letter (Life of Constantine II.69, as Robertson reports): Alexander's question to his clergy on a passage of Scripture; Philostorgius through Photius: a presbyter nicknamed Baucalis. Robertson: the origin is obscure

contested_claims.claim: The cause of Arius's sudden death
contested_claims.sides: Sozomen, as Robertson reports: his friends blamed magic; Alexander's side, with Athanasius, God's judgment; most people a weak heart

absent_details.note: No held source gives it. Robertson reports, with 'We are told', that he was a native of Libya.

absent_details.detail: A copy of the Thalia or his letters in his followers' own hands
absent_details.note: His words survive through his opponents (Theodoret of Cyrus, Athanasius). Philostorgius's friendly history survives only in Photius's hostile epitome.

claims.claim: Egyptian monk whom Gennadius calls founder of the Egyptian monasteries, at the head of the Tabennesiot houses
claims.witness: Gennadius in Jerome, On Illustrious Men 7; Palladius, Lausiac History 32; Sozomen III.14 (following Palladius)

claims.claim: Gave his houses a common rule binding meals, dress, work and prayer
claims.witness: Palladius, Lausiac History 32; Sozomen III.14; the surviving rule collections

claims.claim: Said an angel gave him the rule on a tablet
claims.witness: Palladius, Lausiac History 32 (and the Ethiopic rule's own opening); Sozomen III.14; Gennadius 7 ("received by angelic dictation")

claims.claim: Seven thousand monks lived under the rule in Palladius's day; the first house held 1,300
claims.witness: Palladius, Lausiac History 32

claims.claim: A women's house kept the same rule across the river
claims.witness: Palladius, Lausiac History 33; the Ethiopic rules, Part II

claims.claim: Macarius of Alexandria was admitted in disguise and out-fasted the brothers through Lent
claims.witness: Palladius, Lausiac History 18 (one witness)

claims.claim: Born about 292, died 348
claims.witness: George Schodde's introduction; Ernest Cushing Richardson's note to Gennadius 7 (npnf203)

contested_claims.claim: The angel-and-tablet origin of the rule, and the lettered groups of monks
contested_claims.sides: Palladius, Sozomen and Gennadius report the angel; Ladeuze (via Clarke) held the angel legendary and the lettered groups Palladius's own invention, trusting the Greek Lives over the rule; Butler did not accept Ladeuze's low view of Palladius's rule and called it "probably the most authentic epitome"

absent_details.detail: Any writing in Pachomius's own words
absent_details.note: No writing held here is certainly his own; Schodde thinks the first part of the Ethiopic rules, which is the same as the Greek form, comes close to him; the collections differ, and his life is told by Palladius and by Sozomen after him

claims.claim: Gave away his inheritance after hearing the Gospel read in church, and withdrew to live as an ascetic
claims.witness: Life of Antony 2-3 (attributed to Athanasius) (one hagiographic witness)

claims.claim: Withdrew by stages to the tombs, a deserted fort, and the inner mountain, drawing monks after him
claims.witness: Life of Antony 8-14, 49-50 (one hagiographic witness)

claims.claim: Served the confessors at Alexandria under the persecution of Maximinus, seeking martyrdom
claims.witness: Life of Antony 46-47

claims.claim: Came to Alexandria about 338 to denounce the Arians
claims.witness: Life of Antony 69-70 (the Festal Index date)

claims.claim: Constantine and his sons wrote to him; he answered without elation
claims.witness: Life of Antony 81

claims.claim: Born at Coma, near Heraclea
claims.witness: Sozomen I.13

claims.claim: Sent seven letters in Coptic to monasteries, later translated into Greek
claims.witness: Jerome, On Illustrious Men 88

claims.claim: Died at near a hundred and five, about 356, and was buried secretly at his own request
claims.witness: Life of Antony 89-92 (one hagiographic witness); the years 251 to 356 in Richardson's note to Jerome 88

claims.claim: Two court officials read the Life and resolved to serve God; hearing of Antony moved Augustine
claims.witness: Augustine, Confessions VIII.6, 12

contested_claims.claim: Whether Athanasius of Alexandria wrote the Life of Antony
contested_claims.sides: The long tradition and the balance of opinion give it to Athanasius; Robertson keeps the question open but judges the external evidence too strong to set the work aside as spurious; Weingarten and others attacked its authorship, and Gwatkin went so far as to pronounce that Antony 'never existed,' which Robertson calls far ahead of the evidence

contested_claims.claim: Whether the Life's writer was himself Antony's attendant
contested_claims.sides: The text Robertson prints makes the writer the attendant who "poured water on his hands"; Robertson notes that some Greek and Latin manuscripts make the attendant someone else, and that the text requires further sifting

absent_details.note: Jerome says his seven Coptic letters were translated into Greek; none is held in this Library, so his voice cannot be checked here against the hagiographic Life

claims.claim: A Roman captive who became a royal official in the kingdom of Axum and gathered Christians there
claims.witness: Rufinus, Church History X.9 (from Edesius); retold by Socrates I.19, Sozomen II.24, Theodoret I.23

claims.claim: Consecrated first bishop of Axum by Athanasius of Alexandria
claims.witness: Rufinus X.10 (from Edesius); independently, the emperor Constantius's letter in Athanasius, Apology to Constantius 31 ("advanced to his present rank by Athanasius"); Athanasius's own "Bishop of Auxumis" (Apology 29)

claims.claim: Called the Abba Salama of Axum, meaning the Father of Peace
claims.witness: Hartranft (note to Sozomen II.24); the Dictionary of Christian Biography, quoted in Jackson's note to Theodoret I.23

claims.claim: Consecrated soon after Athanasius became bishop (c.328)
claims.witness: Rufinus X.10

claims.claim: Consecrated later, under Constantius
claims.witness: Valesius (in Zenos's note to Socrates I.19); Robertson, following Gwatkin (prolegomena to Athanasius)

claims.claim: Constantius tried to have Frumentius replaced by the Arian Theophilus, without success
claims.witness: Dictionary of Christian Biography, quoted in Jackson's note to Theodoret I.23 (not in Apology 31 itself)

contested_claims.claim: When Frumentius was consecrated bishop of Axum
contested_claims.sides: Rufinus places it soon after Athanasius became bishop, in 328; Valesius, and Robertson following Gwatkin, place it later under Constantius, since the dates in the story and the emperor's letter fit a later year

absent_details.note: Not given in any held source.
None are held or attested; his life is known only through others.

claims.claim: Ordained deacon at Antioch by Leontius about 350 and soon suspended after an uproar
claims.witness: Athanasius (Robertson's prolegomena); Philostorgius; Socrates II.35

claims.claim: Nicknamed Atheus (the godless) by his own Arian side
claims.witness: Socrates, Church History II.35

claims.claim: Taught that the Son is unlike the Father (the Anomoean position)
claims.witness: His Syntagmation in Epiphanius, Panarion 76; Socrates; Sozomen

claims.claim: Relied on Aristotle's Categories in his arguments
claims.witness: Socrates II.35 (a hostile witness); Athanasius (Robertson)

claims.claim: Deposed from the diaconate at the Council of Constantinople in 360 by his own party
claims.witness: Sozomen IV.23; Athanasius (Robertson): offered as 'a sacrifice to the Emperor's scruples'

claims.claim: Recalled by the emperor Julian, given land on Lesbos, and died at Constantinople
claims.witness: Philostorgius (a partisan witness); Socrates III.5 on the recall by Julian

claims.claim: His pupil Eunomius carried his teaching on, and the sect was named the Eunomians
claims.witness: Socrates II.35 and III.x; Sozomen

absent_details.detail: The years of Aetius's birth and death
absent_details.note: No held source gives either. Philostorgius places his death at Constantinople, after Julian's reign (361-363).

absent_details.detail: The early life of the poor goldsmith who rose by logic
absent_details.note: This account is Philostorgius's, a partisan who praised Aetius, surviving only in Photius's hostile summary.

claims.claim: Bishop of Poitiers in Aquitania and the leading Latin defender of the Nicene faith
claims.witness: His own works (npnf209); Jerome, Lives 100; Watson's life

claims.claim: Condemned at the Council of Beziers in 356 and banished to Phrygia
claims.witness: Watson's life; Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle II.42-45

claims.claim: Wrote twelve books against the Arians (On the Trinity), begun in exile
claims.witness: Jerome, Lives 100; Rufinus's account quoted by Watson

claims.claim: Appealed to Constantius at Constantinople after the Council of Seleucia and was sent back to Gaul
claims.witness: Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle II.45; Watson's life

claims.claim: Confronted Auxentius of Milan before an imperial commission under Valentinian
claims.witness: Hilary, Against Auxentius (his own account); Watson

claims.claim: Cleared Gaul of heresy after Ariminum
claims.witness: Sulpicius Severus, Chronicle II.45 (firmly on Hilary's side)

claims.claim: Born about 300; died about 367
claims.witness: Watson's life, reasoning from Hilary's own words and Sulpicius Severus

claims.claim: Named by Augustine with Cyprian and Lactantius as bringing pagan learning into the church
claims.witness: Augustine, On Christian Doctrine II.40

absent_details.detail: Hilary's parents, upbringing, marriage and age at baptism
absent_details.note: Watson says none of this can be known; Hilary is silent about himself and is never named by Athanasius.

absent_details.detail: The daughter Abra named in a letter printed with his works
absent_details.note: Now generally abandoned as legendary, Watson says.

claims.claim: Bishop of Cagliari sent by Liberius of Rome to Constantius, who refused to condemn Athanasius and was exiled 355-361
claims.witness: Jerome, Lives 95; Fremantle's introduction to Jerome's Dialogue; Theodoret II.12 with Jackson's note

claims.claim: Wrote pamphlets against Constantius in exile and sent the emperor a copy
claims.witness: Jerome, Lives 95; the Latin Opuscula (Hartel), with the letter of Florentius asking whether Lucifer sent the book; Jackson's note to Theodoret

claims.claim: Consecrated Paulinus bishop at Antioch after the exiles' return, instead of joining the council at Alexandria
claims.witness: Socrates III.6 and III.9; Theodoret, Book 3; Fremantle

claims.claim: Would not restore former Arians to office, beginning the Luciferian schism
claims.witness: Socrates III.9; Fremantle's introduction to Jerome's Dialogue, quoting an unnamed source on the principle

claims.claim: Died about 370 or 371
claims.witness: Jerome's Chronicle (371; not held), as reported by Fremantle and Jackson; Richardson's note to Lives 95 gives 370

claims.claim: How far Lucifer was truly a schismatic
claims.witness: J. Ll. Davies (Dictionary of Christian Biography, quoted by Jackson): obscure; Socrates III.9 (he kept the church's teaching); Ambrose and Augustine (schism), via Fremantle; Jerome (saintly, but blamed for the split)

contested_claims.claim: Whether Lucifer was a true schismatic
contested_claims.sides: Socrates says he kept to the church's teaching while his followers stayed apart, and Jerome calls him saintly though he blames him for the split; Ambrose and Augustine, as Fremantle reports, say he fell into schism; J. Ll. Davies calls the extent obscure

absent_details.detail: The reports that Lucifer acted from love of glory or from a grudge against Eusebius of Vercelli
absent_details.note: Jerome reports these but says he does not believe them.

claims.claim: Born at Thabatha near Gaza; studied at Alexandria; visited Antony and adopted the desert life
claims.witness: Jerome, Life of Hilarion 2-4; Sozomen III.14

claims.claim: Settled as a hermit on the coast near Gaza and was the first monk of Palestine
claims.witness: Jerome, Life of Hilarion 14 ("It was he who originated this mode of life and devotion"); Sozomen III.14

claims.claim: Healed the three sons of Aristaenete at Gaza
claims.witness: Jerome, Life of Hilarion 14 (one witness, hagiographic)

claims.claim: Grieved at the crowds his fame drew and left Palestine, moving through Egypt, Sicily and Dalmatia
claims.witness: Jerome, Life of Hilarion 29-43

claims.claim: Died on Cyprus in his eightieth year, about 371
claims.witness: Jerome, Life of Hilarion 44-45; Chester Hartranft's introduction to Sozomen (about 371)

claims.claim: Cured Alaphion near Gaza; it was said that Alaphion's household and Sozomen's grandfather were converted through Hilarion
claims.witness: Sozomen V.15 ("It is said"; his own family tradition)

claims.claim: Epiphanius of Salamis wrote an early letter in his praise
claims.witness: Jerome, Life of Hilarion 1

absent_details.detail: Any writing in Hilarion's own words
absent_details.note: None is held; the Life is Jerome's and is openly hagiographic, and Sozomen gives a separate notice
